# Incident Reporting Coverage Gap: What Real Harms Never Make It Into Any Mandatory Channel?

**Problem:** Multiple jurisdictions are introducing AI incident-reporting requirements, but a structural failure mode is that mandatory channels capture only narrow incident types (e.g. serious systemic-risk events from GPAI providers), while most real-world harms in the AIID fall outside any mandate. The coverage gap has not been quantified against an actual harm corpus.

**Direction:** Quantify the reporting coverage gap. Take a sample of AIID incidents and code each against the reporting criteria of 2-3 emerging regimes (EU AI Act serious-incident reporting, a US framework, etc.): would this incident have been legally required to be reported? Compute the share of real documented harms that fall through the cracks and characterize the systematic blind spots (e.g. consumer harms, bias, non-frontier systems).

**Why it matters:** Effective national incident-response (the NTSB-for-AI open problem) requires reporting mandates that actually catch the harms occurring. Showing the gap between real incidents and reportable incidents directly shapes how reporting thresholds should be set. AIID + public regulatory text — no compute, independent.

**Relevant context:** CSET 'AI Incidents: Key Components for a Mandatory Reporting Regime'; Convergence Analysis AI Incident Reporting landscape; AIID 1,100+ incidents; EU AI Act serious-incident reporting.

# Cross-Lab Safety Eval Disagreement: When Different Public Evals Rank the Same Models Differently

**Problem:** Different public safety evaluations claim to measure overlapping constructs (e.g. 'harmlessness', 'jailbreak robustness'), yet may rank the same models in conflicting orders — a failure mode that undermines any governance regime relying on 'pass an eval'. The degree of cross-eval disagreement is not well characterized for governance audiences.

**Direction:** Characterize eval disagreement. Select 4-6 small open models and 3-4 distinct public safety evals targeting similar constructs. Run all evals on all models on a single GPU, then compute rank correlations between evals. Identify pairs of evals that disagree and inspect example items to explain why (different harm taxonomies, scoring, prompt styles). Report whether 'the model is safe' is eval-dependent.

**Why it matters:** International consensus on evaluation methodology is an explicit open problem (INAISI). Demonstrating that current evals disagree on rankings is direct evidence that a single eval can't anchor governance decisions and that standardization is needed. Small open models, public evals, single GPU — independent and reproducible.

**Relevant context:** INAISI consensus-methodology open problem; Safetywashing on benchmark correlations; Safety Under Scaffolding on condition-dependence.

# Distillation as a Threshold Bypass: Can a Tiny Student Inherit Regulated Capability From a Big Teacher?

**Problem:** Model reuse via distillation is named as a compute-threshold loophole: a small, sub-threshold student model can inherit much of a large teacher's capability, escaping systemic-risk obligations. The boundary — how much regulated capability transfers cheaply — is rarely demonstrated concretely for governance readers.

**Direction:** Probe the distillation-transfer boundary on a feasible slice. Using an existing open small model and a larger open teacher (or public teacher-generated outputs), do a lightweight distillation-style fine-tune on a single GPU for one narrow capability, and measure how much of the teacher's performance the tiny student captures per unit of (sub-threshold) compute. Frame results as 'effective regulated capability acquired below the threshold'. (Scope: small models only, short runs, no from-scratch training.)

**Why it matters:** It concretely shows regulators that training-compute thresholds can be sidestepped by reuse, supporting the case for capability- or behavior-based triggers. Uses only small open models and short single-GPU fine-tunes — within beginner reach and fully counterfactual to lab work. Marked lower-confidence due to the light fine-tuning component.

**Relevant context:** Compute-threshold loophole taxonomy (fine-tuning, distillation, model expansion, inference scaling) in arXiv 2502.00003; DeepSeek-R1 efficiency result; EU/US thresholds.

# Promise vs Practice in Watermarking: Does AI-Content Transparency Survive Trivial Edits?

**Problem:** The EU Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content leans on labeling/watermarking commitments. A known failure mode is that detectable provenance signals (watermarks, metadata) are fragile to trivial transformations (paraphrase, screenshot, re-encode), making the transparency commitment hollow. The robustness of available open watermarking/detection to simple edits is undercharacterized for policy audiences.

**Direction:** Stress-test provenance robustness as the failure mode. Using an open text watermarking scheme (or open AI-text detectors) on a single GPU, generate watermarked/AI text, then apply simple, realistic edits (paraphrasing with a small model, synonym swaps, truncation, format changes) and measure detection survival. Report the edit budget at which transparency signals break and characterize which edits defeat them most cheaply.

**Why it matters:** Transparency-of-AI-content rules assume provenance signals persist; if a screenshot or paraphrase erases them, the regulation can't achieve its goal. Quantifying fragility gives the EU AI Office concrete evidence on what to require. Open tools, small models, single GPU — independent and policy-relevant.

**Relevant context:** EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content; watermark-robustness and AI-text-detection literature; transparency obligations under EU AI Act Article 50.

# Who Audits the Auditors: Mapping Conflict-of-Interest Structures in the Emerging AI Audit Market

**Problem:** Audit-washing arises when second-party auditors cater to paying clients and first-party audits internalize the auditee's interests. As a commercial AI-audit market emerges, the structural conflict-of-interest patterns (who pays, who selects scope, who can publish negative findings) are not systematically mapped — a governance failure mode hiding in plain sight.

**Direction:** Characterize conflict structures across the audit ecosystem. Compile a sample of organizations offering AI audits/assurance and code each on independence dimensions: funding source (paid by auditee vs not), scope control, publication rights, certification incentives, and revolving-door ties. Build a simple taxonomy of conflict configurations and quantify how many actors sit in high-conflict arrangements. Compare against safeguards from mature audit professions (financial, safety-critical).

**Why it matters:** Third-party audit is the proposed backbone of AI accountability, but it fails silently if incentives are misaligned. A structural map gives policymakers the evidence to mandate independence safeguards before the market ossifies. Pure desk research on public information — no compute, classic independent governance scholarship.

**Relevant context:** Outsider Oversight (arXiv 2206.04737); GMF 'AI Audit-Washing and Accountability'; TechPolicy.Press on mandated third-party audits; CCG blog on audit access/roadblocks.

# Definitional Drift: How Inconsistently Do Major AI Policies Define 'Frontier', 'Systemic Risk', and 'High-Risk'?

**Problem:** Core governance terms — 'frontier model', 'systemic risk', 'high-risk', 'general-purpose AI' — anchor binding obligations, but each framework (EU AI Act, US EO, UK approach, lab frameworks) defines them differently or not at all. This definitional drift is a failure mode that lets the same model be in-scope in one regime and out in another, and it has not been systematically tabulated.

**Direction:** Characterize definitional drift across regimes. Extract the operative definitions of 5-6 key terms from ~6-8 governance documents, normalize them, and build a comparison matrix showing where definitions overlap, conflict, or are absent. Then take a few concrete real models and test how each regime classifies them — quantifying how often the same system gets contradictory regulatory statuses.

**Why it matters:** International coordination on AI governance is impossible if the foundational definitions don't align. A precise drift map is directly actionable for harmonization efforts (INAISI, treaty design) and shows where a model can fall through every net. Pure document analysis — no model, no compute, classic independent policy work.

**Relevant context:** EU AI Act GPAI/systemic-risk definitions; US EO compute-based definitions; 'International Agreements on AI Safety' (arXiv 2503.18956); Open Problems in Technical AI Governance.

# The Red-Teaming Black Box: Do Published Safety Reports Disclose Enough to Trust Their Red-Team Claims?

**Problem:** Seoul commitments and frontier frameworks promise internal and external red-teaming, and labs cite red-teaming as evidence of safety. But a failure mode is that red-team disclosures omit the information needed to assess rigor (who, how many prompts, what coverage, what was found and fixed), making the claim unfalsifiable. The disclosure quality has not been systematically scored.

**Direction:** Score red-teaming disclosure quality. Build a rubric of what a credible red-team report should disclose (independence of red-teamers, methodology, scope/coverage, quantitative findings, remediation, residual risk). Apply it to the publicly available safety reports/system cards of ~8-12 recent model releases and grade each. Identify the systematically-omitted elements and which labs disclose most/least.

**Why it matters:** Red-teaming is a headline pillar of voluntary commitments and emerging regulation; if reports are too opaque to evaluate, the pillar is decorative. A disclosure scorecard tells regulators exactly what to require for red-teaming to be auditable — the third-party-verification open problem. Public reports only, no compute, independent.

**Relevant context:** Seoul commitments (red-teaming + info sharing); METR common elements; AI Transparency Atlas disclosure deficits; Outsider Oversight on audit access.

# Patterns of Responsibility: Who Gets Blamed (and Who Escapes) After AI Harms?

**Problem:** Following AI harms, responsibility is diffuse across developers, deployers, and users, and a governance failure mode is that accountability systematically lands on the wrong (or weakest) party while developers escape. Recent work began mapping responsibility patterns from incidents, but the distribution across actor types and harm categories is not fully characterized for policy use.

**Direction:** Characterize responsibility-attribution patterns. Using a sample of AIID incidents (or the responsibility-annotated subset), code each for which actor was held responsible (developer / deployer / user / no one) and the harm type. Quantify the distribution and test whether developers are under-attributed relative to their causal role. Identify harm categories where accountability systematically fails to attach to anyone.

**Why it matters:** Liability allocation is a core governance lever; if blame predictably misses upstream developers, regulation needs to redistribute responsibility. Grounding this in observed incidents (not theory) gives liability scholars and regulators empirical traction. Public incident data, no compute, fully independent.

**Relevant context:** 'From Incidents to Insights: Patterns of Responsibility following AI Harms' (arXiv 2505.04291); AIID; Medium analysis of AIID liability ($2.9B figure).

# Stale by Design: Measuring How Fast Fixed Compute Thresholds Decay Against the Efficiency Frontier

**Problem:** A structural failure mode of compute-threshold governance is that a fixed FLOP line becomes increasingly permissive as algorithmic efficiency improves — last year's frontier capability is reachable below threshold today. The decay rate of threshold effectiveness has not been empirically estimated from public capability/compute trends for a policy audience.

**Direction:** Estimate the threshold-decay rate. Using Epoch AI compute and capability data, fit the trend of 'compute needed to reach a fixed capability level' over time. Project how a static 10^25 threshold's coverage of frontier-equivalent capability shrinks year over year, and estimate the doubling time of the threshold's permissiveness. Translate into 'how often a fixed threshold would need to be lowered to hold capability coverage constant'.

**Why it matters:** It quantifies, for compute-governance designers, exactly how badly fixed thresholds erode and how aggressively they'd need indexing to stay meaningful — directly informing dynamic-threshold design (Epoch AI, MIRI agenda). Uses only public Epoch trend data and basic regression — beginner statistics, no compute, fully counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Context note that fixed thresholds become permissive as efficiency advances; Epoch AI compute tracking; DeepSeek-R1 efficiency result; compute-threshold limitation analyses.

# A HACCP-Style Hazard-Analysis Audit of Frontier Safety Frameworks

**Problem:** Frontier AI safety frameworks describe risk-management processes, but it is unclear whether they actually specify *where* in the development/deployment lifecycle a hazard is caught and controlled. Vague commitments leave gaps with no defined control point.

**Direction:** Import HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) from food safety. Build a coding rubric mapping each commitment in the 12+ published safety frameworks to a lifecycle stage and asking: is there a defined Critical Control Point (a specific monitoring step + threshold + corrective action)? Hand-code all frameworks, score % of hazards with a complete CCP triple, and visualize coverage gaps across companies.

**Why it matters:** Turns a fuzzy 'is this framework good' question into a structured, reproducible audit any third party can run on public documents. Surfaces systematic gaps (e.g., hazards named but never monitored) that regulators and the EU AI Office care about. No lab access needed.

**Relevant context:** HACCP Codex guidelines (FAO); 12 published frontier safety frameworks (arXiv 2512.01166 'Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks'); EU Code of Practice safety chapter.

# Vagueness Metrics from Privacy-Policy Linguistics Applied to AI Safety Commitments

**Problem:** AI safety frameworks and the EU Code of Practice are criticized as vague, but vagueness is asserted rather than measured. Without a metric, 'this commitment is too weak' is unfalsifiable.

**Direction:** Transfer the obfuscating-word/vagueness lexicon methodology used to measure privacy-policy vagueness (counting hedges like 'might', 'where appropriate', 'state-of-the-art') into a Python pipeline. Compile a corpus of public safety frameworks + the Code of Practice, compute vagueness density, readability grade, and commitment-strength scores per sentence, and compare across companies and over time.

**Why it matters:** Gives policymakers a cheap, reproducible specificity score to track whether voluntary commitments are tightening or de-specifying. Directly addresses the open problem of the gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2511.21758 (longitudinal vagueness measurement of LLM privacy policies, ~75% of sentences contain obfuscating words); CSET EU Code of Safety analysis; framework corpus is fully public.

# Aviation Near-Miss Taxonomy Transferred to the AI Incident Database

**Problem:** Aviation safety advanced largely because it records *near-misses and precursors*, not just accidents. The AI Incident Database mostly captures realized harms, missing the precursor signal that aviation relies on.

**Direction:** Borrow the ASRS/NTSB precursor-vs-accident taxonomy. Pull the public AI Incident Database, write a Python classifier (keyword + small open LLM zero-shot) tagging each record as accident vs near-miss vs precursor, and measure how thin the precursor layer is. Propose a near-miss reporting schema modeled on ASRS.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates empirically that AI incident reporting lacks the early-warning layer that made aviation safe, supporting the case for an NTSB-style AI incident regime. Uses only public data.

**Relevant context:** AI Incident Database (public); arXiv 2507.23669 (semantic association of AIID reports); arXiv 2503.19887 (AI incident regime); ASRS aviation reporting model.

# An AIBOM Completeness Audit of Hugging Face Model Cards

**Problem:** Software supply-chain governance relies on a Bill of Materials. AI 'Bills of Materials' (AIBOM) are being standardized (CISA/G7, OWASP), but we don't know how much of the required AIBOM information real model cards actually contain.

**Direction:** Transfer the SBOM completeness-audit concept. Use the OWASP AIBOM field schema (models, datasets, code, hardware, data processing, governance), scrape a sample of public Hugging Face model cards via the API, and score each card's AIBOM completeness per field. Report which fields are systematically missing across the ecosystem.

**Why it matters:** Provides an empirical baseline for AI supply-chain transparency policy: regulators proposing AIBOM mandates need to know the current gap. Pure public-data analysis, no training.

**Relevant context:** CISA/G7 SBOM-for-AI guidance; OWASP AIBOM project + ALOHA generator (ACM 10.1145/3756681.3756998); IBM AI bill of materials; Hugging Face API.

# Central-Bank Stress-Test Scenario Templates Applied to Frontier AI Safety Cases

**Problem:** Financial regulators force banks through standardized adverse scenarios; frontier AI safety cases instead let each company choose its own threat scenarios, making them incomparable and easy to game.

**Direction:** Import the structured stress-test scenario format (a fixed set of escalating adverse scenarios with required responses). Construct 3-4 standardized AI misuse/loss-of-control scenarios, then hand-code whether each public safety framework's commitments would 'pass' each scenario, producing a stress-test scorecard. Analyze where frameworks are silent.

**Why it matters:** Makes safety cases comparable across companies via a common scenario battery, mirroring how bank stress tests created comparability. Strategically valuable governance infrastructure doable on public docs.

**Relevant context:** FSB 'Financial Stability Implications of AI'; arXiv 2511.21838 (qualitative+quantitative frontier risk); arXiv 2512.01166 (frontier safety framework evaluation); Fed/ECB stress-test methodology.

# Mutation Testing for AI Safety Benchmarks: How Robust Is a 'Pass'?

**Problem:** Governance increasingly relies on benchmark scores as evidence of safety, but a benchmark 'pass' may be brittle to trivial rephrasings — meaning a regulator's evidentiary basis is fragile.

**Direction:** Transfer mutation testing from software engineering. Take a small public safety/refusal benchmark, write a set of semantics-preserving mutation operators (paraphrase, reorder, add filler) applied to prompts via a small open model, and measure how much a model's safety pass-rate shifts under mutation. Report a 'benchmark fragility' score usable as a verification heuristic.

**Why it matters:** Directly addresses the open problem of verifiable, reproducible safety claims: shows whether benchmark-based safety evidence survives perturbation. Counterfactually valuable — labs deprioritize meta-evaluation of their own metrics.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2407.00125 (fault injection in AI systems, DeepCrime mutation operators); arXiv 2504.04372 (mutation-inspired LLM evaluation); 'fragile safety claim' framing from frontier auditing literature.

# Clinical-Trial Preregistration Schema for AI Safety Evaluations

**Problem:** Medicine curbed selective reporting via preregistration (CONSORT, registered reports). AI safety evaluations are reported post-hoc, enabling cherry-picking of which evals to run and disclose — a governance blind spot.

**Direction:** Adapt the CONSORT-AI / preregistration template into a concrete preregistration schema for safety evals (hypotheses, eval set, thresholds, stopping rules declared in advance). Then audit a sample of published model/system cards for how many of these elements were plausibly fixed before vs after seeing results, scoring 'preregisterability'.

**Why it matters:** Imports a proven anti-gaming mechanism from clinical science into AI governance and quantifies how far current practice is from it. All on public documents; no lab cooperation required.

**Relevant context:** CONSORT-AI extension (PMC8183333); preregistration/registered reports literature; published frontier model/system cards.

# Epidemiological R0 Model for Open-Weight Capability Proliferation

**Problem:** Compute and weight-proliferation governance lacks a simple quantitative model of how fast a frontier capability spreads to open-weight reproductions, making timelines for 'when does this become ungovernable' hand-wavy.

**Direction:** Transfer the epidemiological reproduction-number / diffusion model. Assemble a public dataset of frontier capability milestones and the dates open-weight models reached comparable scores (from leaderboards/Epoch), then fit a simple diffusion curve and estimate an effective 'proliferation R0' and lag time per capability.

**Why it matters:** Gives compute-governance debates a tractable, data-grounded diffusion estimate (how much lead time governance has) instead of intuition. Uses only public leaderboard/Epoch data.

**Relevant context:** Epoch AI compute/capability tracking; R0 estimation (PLOS One 10.1371/journal.pone.0000282); MIRI compute governance agenda; open-weight leaderboards.

# Treaty-Verification Checklist from Arms Control Applied to AI Commitments

**Problem:** International AI coordination borrows the *language* of arms control but rarely the *verification engineering*. Most AI commitments lack the verifiability features that made arms-control treaties enforceable.

**Direction:** Transfer the arms-control verification taxonomy (declared baselines, on-site inspection rights, remote monitoring, challenge inspections, non-compliance triggers). Build a rubric and score a corpus of public AI commitments (Frontier AI Safety Commitments, Code of Practice, Bletchley/Seoul declarations) on which verification features they contain.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies the verifiability gap in current international AI agreements, directly serving the open problem of third-party-auditable safety claims and international coordination. Public-document analysis.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2004.07213 (Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims); Schelling & Halperin 'Strategy and Arms Control'; Frontier AI Safety Commitments; International Network of AI Safety Institutes.

# Semantic Network Analysis of How 'AI Safety' Is Framed Across Jurisdictions

**Problem:** The UK→'Security Institute' vs US→'CAISI/innovation' rebrandings hint that 'safety' means different things across governments, but this is anecdotal. Divergent framings can fragment international coordination.

**Direction:** Transfer semantic network analysis from political science/securitization studies. Build a corpus of official AI policy texts (US, EU, UK, China translations) and compute co-occurrence networks around 'safety/security/innovation/risk', comparing which concepts cluster in each jurisdiction. Visualize divergence.

**Why it matters:** Empirically maps where international consensus on AI evaluation/safety is semantically possible vs blocked — a prerequisite for the open problem of international coordination. Public texts only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2601.04107 (comparative semantic network analysis of AI securitisation US/EU/China); UK AISI/CAISI rebranding; semantic network methods.

# Fault-Tree Analysis (from Reliability Engineering) of a Loss-of-Control Scenario

**Problem:** Governance discussions about catastrophic AI risk rarely decompose a scenario into the chain of failures that must co-occur, so it's hard to identify which governance interventions break the chain most cheaply.

**Direction:** Transfer Fault Tree Analysis from nuclear/aerospace reliability. Pick one documented threat model (e.g., a model exfiltrating its weights), decompose it into a fault tree of necessary intermediate failures, annotate each node with which existing governance mechanism (if any) addresses it, and compute minimal cut sets to find the leverage points.

**Why it matters:** Translates abstract catastrophe narratives into a structured intervention map regulators can act on — operationalizing safety objectives into deployment controls. Pure analysis, no compute.

**Relevant context:** Fault Tree Analysis (NUREG reliability standard); dynamic safety cases (arXiv 2412.17618); Open Problems in Technical AI Governance operationalization gap.

# Financial 'Know-Your-Customer' Patterns Applied to Compute Provider Governance

**Problem:** Compute governance proposals invoke KYC-style rules for cloud/compute providers, but there's no structured comparison of what financial KYC actually requires versus what compute KYC proposals specify.

**Direction:** Transfer the AML/KYC tiered due-diligence framework from banking. Build a side-by-side rubric (customer identification, risk tiering, transaction monitoring, suspicious-activity reporting, thresholds) and code which elements appear in published compute-governance proposals. Identify which KYC components have no compute analogue yet.

**Why it matters:** Gives compute-governance design a mature, battle-tested template and reveals concrete gaps, addressing the open problem of compute mechanisms balancing safety and innovation. Document analysis only.

**Relevant context:** FATF/AML-KYC tiered due diligence; Epoch/MIRI compute governance agenda; Heim et al. compute governance writing.

# Cochrane-Style Systematic-Review Methodology for the AI Safety Index

**Problem:** The FLI AI Safety Index scores labs, but its methodology is a single-pass expert judgment. Evidence-based medicine developed rigorous systematic-review protocols (inclusion criteria, evidence grading, inter-rater reliability) that the Index doesn't use.

**Direction:** Transfer Cochrane/GRADE systematic-review machinery. Re-score one Safety Index dimension for several labs using an explicit inclusion-criteria + evidence-grading protocol, compute inter-rater reliability against the published scores using two independent coders (or two LLM passes), and report where the rigorous protocol disagrees with the Index.

**Why it matters:** Strengthens a widely-cited governance benchmark with reproducible evidence-grading, advancing international consensus on evaluation methodology. Builds directly on the strategy hint to extend the AI Safety Index methodology.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index (public methodology + scores); GRADE/Cochrane systematic-review standards; strategy hint FR67 (apply AI Safety Index methodology to additional dimensions).

# Bug-Bounty Economics Applied to AI Vulnerability Disclosure Policy

**Problem:** Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) and bug bounties shaped cybersecurity governance; AI flaw/jailbreak disclosure lacks comparable norms, and we don't know how labs' disclosure policies measure up against mature CVD standards.

**Direction:** Transfer the ISO 29147/30111 CVD framework and bug-bounty design principles. Code a sample of AI companies' public vulnerability/flaw-disclosure and bug-bounty pages against CVD maturity dimensions (scope, safe-harbor, timelines, severity rubric, researcher protections). Score and compare.

**Why it matters:** Maps a proven governance mechanism onto AI and quantifies the gap, supporting incident-response framework development. All on public policy pages; valuable outside any single lab.

**Relevant context:** ISO 29147/30111 CVD standards; AI flaw-disclosure proposals; The Future Society NTSB-for-AI incident-response framing.

# Environmental-Impact-Statement Template for Frontier Model Releases

**Problem:** Environmental law forces an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) before major actions, with public comment. Frontier model releases have no analogous structured pre-release impact disclosure, so societal risks are assessed ad hoc.

**Direction:** Transfer the NEPA EIS structure (scoping, alternatives, affected populations, mitigation, public comment). Convert it into an 'AI Release Impact Statement' template, then retroactively populate it for 2-3 recent model releases using only public information to demonstrate feasibility and surface what data is unavailable.

**Why it matters:** Offers a concrete, transferable operationalization of safety objectives into a deployment practice with public accountability. The retroactive exercise reveals the disclosure gap. No compute or lab access.

**Relevant context:** NEPA EIS process; EU AI Act systemic-risk assessment requirements; FDA-for-AI approval-regulation debate (arXiv 2408.00821).

# Survival Analysis (from Epidemiology) of Safety-Commitment Persistence

**Problem:** AI labs make public safety commitments, but some are quietly walked back. There is no quantitative study of how long commitments 'survive' — a key signal for whether voluntary governance is durable.

**Direction:** Transfer survival analysis / Kaplan-Meier estimation. Build a longitudinal dataset of dated public commitments (from archived framework versions via the Wayback Machine), code each as 'still in force', 'weakened', or 'removed' at later snapshots, and fit a survival curve estimating median commitment lifetime and hazard of weakening.

**Why it matters:** Provides hard evidence on the durability of voluntary commitments, central to the open problem of moving from voluntary codes to enforceable standards. Uses only public archived documents.

**Relevant context:** Kaplan-Meier survival analysis; archived safety-framework versions (Wayback Machine); EU AI Office voluntary-vs-enforceable gap.

# Defense-in-Depth Layer Mapping (from Nuclear/Cybersecurity) of Deployment Safeguards

**Problem:** Nuclear and cyber safety use explicit 'defense in depth' layering (independent barriers). AI deployment safeguards are described as lists, not as independent layers, so single-point-of-failure risks are invisible.

**Direction:** Transfer the defense-in-depth barrier model. From public deployment-safety descriptions, classify each safeguard into a layer (pre-training data, fine-tuning, system prompt, input filter, output filter, monitoring, human review), then assess layer independence and identify where multiple 'layers' actually share a single mechanism (correlated failure).

**Why it matters:** Reveals whether claimed layered defenses are genuinely independent — a verification concern regulators need — without requiring access to the safeguards themselves. Public-document analysis.

**Relevant context:** IAEA defense-in-depth doctrine; published deployment-safety/system-card descriptions; technical AI governance operationalization gap.

# Delphi-Method Consensus Mapping for International AI Evaluation Standards

**Problem:** The International Network of AI Safety Institutes needs consensus on evaluation methodology, but disagreements are scattered across documents. The Delphi method (structured expert-consensus elicitation) is designed exactly for mapping where consensus exists vs not.

**Direction:** Transfer the Delphi structured-consensus framework. Extract concrete evaluation-methodology claims from each AISI's public outputs, organize them into a structured matrix of agree/disagree/silent per institute per claim, and compute a consensus index identifying which methodology points are ripe for standardization.

**Why it matters:** Turns the vague goal of 'international consensus on evaluation methodology' into a measured map of where consensus already exists, directly serving the open problem. Public documents only.

**Relevant context:** Delphi method (RAND); International Network of AI Safety Institutes outputs; UK AISI / US CAISI / EU eval publications.

# Actuarial Loss-Distribution Modeling for AI Incident Severity

**Problem:** Insurance/actuarial science models tail risk via loss distributions, enabling pricing and capital requirements. AI governance lacks an empirical severity distribution for incidents, so 'how heavy is the tail' is unargued.

**Direction:** Transfer actuarial severity-distribution fitting. Code severity for AI Incident Database records on a simple ordinal scale, fit candidate heavy-tailed distributions, and estimate the tail index. Discuss what the tail shape implies for insurability and mandatory-reporting thresholds.

**Why it matters:** Gives governance a quantitative handle on AI tail risk grounded in real incident data, informing incident-reporting thresholds and insurance-based governance. Public data, basic statistics only.

**Relevant context:** Extreme value theory / actuarial loss modeling; AI Incident Database; FSB systemic-risk framing; arXiv 2509.26150 (regulatory incident reporting).

# Software Test-Coverage Metrics Applied to Safety-Framework Threat Coverage

**Problem:** In software, 'test coverage' quantifies how much of the code is exercised. Safety frameworks claim to cover risks, but there's no coverage metric over a canonical threat taxonomy, so coverage claims are unverifiable.

**Direction:** Transfer the coverage-metric concept. Adopt a public risk taxonomy (e.g., MIT AI Risk Repository) as the 'codebase', then map each safety framework's commitments onto taxonomy entries and compute a coverage percentage and a heatmap of which risk categories are systematically uncovered across companies.

**Why it matters:** Produces a standardized, reproducible 'threat coverage score' for safety frameworks, enabling apples-to-apples comparison demanded by regulators. Public taxonomy + public frameworks.

**Relevant context:** MIT AI Risk Repository (public taxonomy); software coverage metrics; arXiv 2512.01166 frontier safety framework evaluation; EU Code of Practice.

# Differential-Diagnosis Reasoning (from Medicine) for AI Incident Causal Attribution

**Problem:** When an AI incident occurs, attributing it to model, deployment, prompt, or user is inconsistent across reports, undermining the learning value of incident databases. Medicine has structured differential-diagnosis protocols for exactly this attribution problem.

**Direction:** Transfer the differential-diagnosis checklist. Build a structured attribution rubric (rule-in/rule-out of candidate causes) and apply it to a sample of AI Incident Database entries with two coders, measuring how often the structured protocol changes the attributed cause versus the original free-text classification.

**Why it matters:** Improves the consistency and analytic value of incident reporting — a prerequisite for an NTSB-style learning regime — using only public incident data and basic inter-rater statistics.

**Relevant context:** Differential-diagnosis methodology (clinical reasoning); AI Incident Database; arXiv 2503.19887 (AI incident regime); aviation occurrence-report NLP (arXiv 2301.05663).

# Antitrust Market-Concentration Metrics Applied to Compute and Model Supply

**Problem:** Regulatory-capture concerns in AI safety hinge on industry concentration, but the AI compute/model market is rarely measured with the standard tools (HHI, concentration ratios) economists use for antitrust.

**Direction:** Transfer the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index and concentration-ratio toolkit. Assemble public data on frontier-model providers and compute/cloud market shares (from Epoch, public reports), compute HHI for distinct layers (chips, cloud, frontier models), and relate concentration to lobbying/regulatory-capture risk.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies the structural concentration that drives regulatory-capture and compute-governance debates, grounding them in standard economic metrics. Public data, basic computation.

**Relevant context:** HHI / antitrust concentration metrics; Springer 'AI safety and regulatory capture' (10.1007/s00146-025-02534-0); Epoch compute tracking; arXiv 2509.22872 (anti-regulatory AI).

# Formal-Methods Specification Audit: Are Safety Commitments Falsifiable?

**Problem:** Formal methods distinguish specifications that are checkable (a clear pass/fail oracle exists) from those that are not. Many safety commitments are written so no observer could ever declare them violated — making them unenforceable.

**Direction:** Transfer the formal-spec notion of testability/falsifiability. For each commitment in a corpus of public frameworks, hand-classify whether a concrete, observable test could in principle determine compliance, and what the oracle would be. Report the fraction of commitments that are operationally falsifiable per company.

**Why it matters:** Gives regulators a sharp filter separating enforceable from decorative commitments, directly addressing the voluntary-vs-enforceable gap. Pure document analysis; high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Formal-methods specification/testability concepts; arXiv 2505.01643 (third-party compliance reviews for safety frameworks); EU AI Office enforceability gap; 'fragile safety claim' framing.

# Process-Mining (from Business Operations) of the Model-Release Decision Workflow

Proposals describe compute governance as a 'pause button', but the issue-to-actually-stopped link assumes enforceable control over distributed, fungible compute, which is undemonstrated.

**Direction:** From the compute-governance literature, decompose the proposed pause mechanism into required preconditions (chip registry, location attestation, kill-switch authority, jurisdiction) and assess, with public evidence, which preconditions currently exist versus are aspirational. Produce a readiness scorecard for the pause-button chain and flag the single weakest precondition.

**Why it matters:** Compute governance is a leading lever for medium/long-horizon catastrophic risk that frontier labs won't build; a clear-eyed audit of which pause-button preconditions are real tells the field where to invest. Pure literature synthesis, no compute, very counterfactual and long-horizon.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2506.20530 'Toward a Global Regime for Compute Governance: Building the Pause Button'; arXiv:2604.04712 hardware-level governance feasibility taxonomy; LessWrong compute governance literature review.
